01_hook: He doesn't play monsters. He lets them in. August seventeenth, nineteen forty-three. Manhattan. A boy born between two painters who had already begun to leave each other. That boy will become one of the most watched faces in cinema, and the man who almost never explains why. This is Robert De Niro. Not the impression. The life underneath.
02_origen: The father, Robert De Niro Senior, was a painter. An abstract expressionist. He studied with Hans Hofmann. Peggy Guggenheim showed him. In nineteen forty-six he had a solo show at Art of This Century, the room where New York was about to change painting. The mother, Virginia Admiral, painted too. Then she mostly stopped, and she raised the child. The marriage, from nineteen forty-two, did not hold. They separated when Robert was about two. The father became a man you sometimes caught on the street, on a bicycle. A second, and he was gone. Years later De Niro said the sentence that explains more than any interview. My father was the real thing. The father kept journals. In them, a private war. He was gay, in a world that punished that truth, and he wrote it down by hand, with guilt. The son did not grow up inside that confession. He grew up beside the silence. In twenty fourteen he produced the documentary Remembering the Artist and read those journals on camera. The man who never talks opened, because the paintings had not been given their due. He said he wanted his father to have his place. That it was his responsibility. When the father was dying of cancer, in nineteen ninety-three, on the day he turned seventy-one, it was the mother, decades divorced from him, who took him in. The son was already the most feared actor in America. He was still the boy who had watched a bicycle turn the corner.
03_oficio: Robert junior was not an easy student. School slipped through his hands. He left high school at sixteen to study the only thing that held him: watching people until he could wear them. Stella Adler taught him that the actor's job is to imagine the life, not to beg for the emotion. Later, Lee Strasberg and the Actors Studio pushed the other door. Memory. Nerve. What is actually at stake. De Niro took both schools and then did something less fashionable. He did the homework. The accent. The weight of the body. The way a man holds a glass. He has never liked the myth of possession. He likes choices. Concrete ones. The kind you can repeat on take twelve. His early films do not ask permission. With Brian De Palma he makes Greetings and Hi, Mom!, strange satires of Vietnam-era New York. In nineteen seventy-three comes Bang the Drum Slowly. He plays a catcher who is dying. The business looks up. The same year, Martin Scorsese puts him in Mean Streets. Johnny Boy. A neighborhood fuse, in Little Italy, smiling as he lights it. Scorsese was not hiring a star. He was hiring a frequency.
04_padrino: Then Francis Ford Coppola asks for the impossible. Play Vito Corleone as a young man, in The Godfather, Part Two. Without doing a Marlon Brando impression. Without sharing the frame with Brando. They shot their halves apart. De Niro learned the Sicilian dialect until the lines sat in his mouth like a language from home. He watched Brando the way a painter studies a canvas from across the room. Not to copy the brush. To understand the weight. Nineteen seventy-five. The Oscar for Best Supporting Actor. He was thirty-one. He did not look like a winner. He looked like a man who had borrowed someone else's youth and returned it undamaged.
05_taxi: Nineteen seventy-six. Taxi Driver. Paul Schrader writes Travis Bickle, an insomniac in a metal coffin, rolling through a city that has come apart. Scorsese directs. De Niro shaves a mohawk, puts on the fatigue jacket, and builds a man so lonely he rehearses friendship in a mirror. You talkin' to me? The line was a seed. He grew the whole interrogation, asking an empty room a question no one was going to answer. Cannes gave the film the Palme d'Or. America gave it a permanent echo. People quote Travis like a joke. The performance is not a joke. It is a diagnosis of a city, and of the kind of man that city keeps manufacturing. On that shoot, Diahnne Abbott has a small role. They marry that same year. Raphael is born. De Niro adopts Abbott's daughter, Drena. For a while, the most isolated character in American movies is, off camera, a husband and a father. He also shoots Bertolucci's Nineteen Hundred, and the next year Scorsese's difficult musical New York, New York, with Liza Minnelli. It was not a hit. De Niro had already stopped letting the box office decide which performance stays.
06_toro: If Taxi Driver was a nerve, Raging Bull was a body. Jake LaMotta. Jealousy as a fighting style. Scorsese did not want to make a boxing picture. De Niro kept bringing him the book. When they finally shot it, in black and white, he did what the legend still resists. First he played the fighter in shape. Then he shut the production down and gained about sixty pounds to play the older, ruined Jake. Not a suit. A decision, lived for months, so the camera would have nothing to forgive. Nineteen eighty-one. The Oscar for Best Actor. People who agree on nothing agree on this. It is one of the great performances in the history of film. In the last scene Jake is alone, shadowboxing, rehearsing, badly, how to be seen. The monster is gone. A man is left practicing a line. Before that, The Deer Hunter, nineteen seventy-eight. Steel country, Vietnam, a wedding long enough to show you what the war will break. Another nomination. His character does not explain the damage. He swallows it. And in nineteen eighty-two, The King of Comedy. Rupert Pupkin, the fan who decides to kidnap fame. People hated it. Time made it a prophecy. In twenty nineteen, in Joker, De Niro steps through the mirror and plays the host, Murray Franklin. Yesterday's stalker is now the man with the microphone.
07_imperio: The eighties and nineties are a map of American unease, and he is at the crossroads. Once Upon a Time in America, by Sergio Leone. The Untouchables: his Al Capone walks into a banquet with a baseball bat and ends a conversation forever. The Mission, with Jeremy Irons: a man hauling his guilt up a waterfall. Brazil, by Terry Gilliam, where he lets himself be physically funny. Midnight Run: a bounty hunter opposite Charles Grodin. The face, it turns out, can be funny without asking permission. Goodfellas, nineteen ninety. Jimmy Conway. King of the neighborhood, and the smile is a warning. The same year, Awakenings, a doctor beside patients the world had filed away. Another nomination. Cape Fear: Max Cady, ink and threat. Another nomination. In nineteen ninety-three he directs for the first time, A Bronx Tale, and plays a father trying to pull his son off the false shine of the street. The neighborhood is not a set. It is the language of his childhood.
08_calor: Nineteen ninety-five. Twice. Casino, with Scorsese again. Ace Rothstein, convinced he can manage the desert. And Heat, by Michael Mann. Neil McCauley, a thief with a monk's discipline. Al Pacino is across the table. They had shared The Godfather, Part Two, without ever sharing a scene. In a Los Angeles diner, two decades of myth sit down for coffee. Neither one blinks. The scene is quiet. That is why it detonates. At the turn of the century, the man who had been America's unease agrees to be America's difficult father-in-law. Meet the Parents. Jack Byrnes. A polygraph in the basement and a smile like a locked door. The movie is a phenomenon. People who never saw Raging Bull now do the stare at dinner. He does not become a mascot. He proves control is also a comic weapon. In Analyze This, the gangster goes to therapy. In Silver Linings Playbook, twenty twelve, he is a superstitious father, suddenly tender. Another nomination. He researches the comedy the way he researches a crime. And in two thousand six he directs The Good Shepherd, a cold film about the birth of the C.I.A. The old subject. What a life of secrets does to a man.
09_casa: Off the set, the biography is not a poster. It is a family with several doors. The marriage to Diahnne Abbott ends in nineteen eighty-eight. With Toukie Smith he has twins in nineteen ninety-five, Julian and Airyn, through a surrogate. In April twenty twenty-five, Airyn speaks publicly as a transgender woman. De Niro's answer is short and clear. He supports her. He loves her as his daughter. No speech. A father, on the record. He marries Grace Hightower in nineteen ninety-seven. Elliot is born in ninety-eight. Helen Grace arrives in twenty eleven, also through a surrogate. They separate in twenty eighteen. He asks for privacy and keeps the sentence that matters. They will go on as partners in raising their children. Around twenty twenty-one he is seen with Tiffany Chen. On April sixth, twenty twenty-three, Gia Virginia Chen-De Niro is born. He is seventy-nine, and he does not announce it. A month later an interviewer counts six children. De Niro corrects him. Seven, actually. I just had a baby. He has said that when he looks at Gia, what is consuming him goes quiet. He wants her to grow up with Chinese and English in the house. Seven children. More than fifty years between the oldest and the youngest. Drena became an actress. Raphael built a life in New York real estate. The others grew up under a last name that arrives before they do. He does not pretend that is simple.
10_tribeca: There is another De Niro. The one who builds rooms for other people. With the chef Nobu Matsuhisa he becomes a partner in Nobu. The first restaurant opens in Tribeca. Downtown stops being only a location in his movies. It becomes a table. A bet on the neighborhood. With Jane Rosenthal he founds Tribeca Productions. After September eleventh, two thousand one, when the dust in lower Manhattan was not a metaphor, they create the Tribeca Film Festival with Craig Hatkoff. A festival as a civic act. Bring the lights back. Bring the audiences back south of Canal Street. He has never been the most sentimental New Yorker at a microphone. He did something harder. He stayed. And he built.
11_tarde: The late performances refuse an easy victory lap. The Irishman, twenty nineteen. Scorsese again, now on Netflix. The digital de-aging works here as a moral instrument: a face moving backward into the crimes, then forward into the nursing home. Frank Sheeran confuses loyalty with erasure. Joe Pesci returns. Pacino is Jimmy Hoffa. De Niro is the silence after the shot. Another nomination. Killers of the Flower Moon, twenty twenty-three. William Hale, the uncle who smiles while a people are killed for the oil under their names. Politeness, used as a weapon. Half a century after Mean Streets, they are still asking what a man will justify in the name of family. Another nomination. Two Oscars. A pile of almosts. He never acted as if the almosts were the point. In twenty twenty-five he plays two mobsters in one body, Frank Costello and Vito Genovese, in The Alto Knights. And in Zero Day, his first series as the lead, he is a former president called back because the country does not understand the attack it suffered. That May, at Cannes, Leonardo DiCaprio hands him an honorary Palme d'Or. De Niro does not talk about himself. He talks about art as a public act, about a democracy he believes has to be defended, and about a tariff on films made outside the United States. Agree or don't. He showed up, and he used the microphone for something other than thanks. In August twenty twenty-six, Netflix releases The Whisper Man. He is Peter Willis, a retired detective and a father called back because children are disappearing, and because his son, played by Adam Scott, has no one else to ask. At eighty-three he is still who they write when the story needs someone who knows where the body is buried.
12_cierre: So what do you do with a life like that. You can list the movies. Vito. Travis. Jake. Capone. Jimmy Conway. Neil McCauley. Jack Byrnes. Frank Sheeran. William Hale. The list is the easy part. The hard part is the boy on a Greenwich Village street who learned, early, that love can be a bicycle going the other way. He spent sixty years learning how to stand still inside other people. Killers, comics, fathers, frauds. Precisely enough that we forget there is an actor in the room. He doesn't interpret the dark. He opens the door and does not step back. Robert De Niro is still watching. And he still does not owe you the explanation.
